title: Variation Theory In Practice
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane opens with the core claim of Variation Theory -- humans pay more attention to what changes than to what stays constant -- and argues it is especially useful when a student is processing something new and needs their attention conserved. He illustrates with a one-on-one example: while a student struggled with rounding ahead of a unit on circles, Kane used a deliberately sequenced set of examples (3.3, 3.4, 3.5, 3.6, 3.7, then a second cluster starting at 11.7) rather than a randomly chosen set, so that each small change in the tenths digit isolated exactly one cause-and-effect relationship for the student to notice. He explains why this matters pedagogically: experienced teachers hold so much background knowledge about a concept like rounding that the number of separate ideas a struggling student must juggle becomes invisible to them, and variation reduces that working-memory load by changing one thing at a time. Kane is explicit that this is a confidence-building first step, not a complete solution -- he flags that follow-up practice must reintroduce variety (different digit counts, different rounding places, edge cases like 999.5) once the student has stabilized. He frames the technique as especially suited to the specific situation of a confused student needing to rebuild confidence, distinct from its more general use as an ongoing practice tool.
points: Kane's rounding sequence (3.3, 3.4, 3.5, 3.6, 3.7, then 11.7, 11.5, 11.4, 11.45) changes only one digit at a time so a struggling student can isolate exactly one cause-and-effect relationship per step.

The technique specifically targets working-memory overload: experienced teachers no longer notice how many separate ideas (place value, rounding direction, digit thresholds) a confused student must hold simultaneously.

Kane is explicit that tightly sequenced variation is a confidence-building first step, not a finished strategy -- follow-up practice must reintroduce variety (different digit counts, rounding places, edge cases) once the student stabilizes.
He credits Craig Barton's tip of carrying a mini-whiteboard while circulating the room as the practical enabler that let him deliver this sequence to one student in real time.
quotes: Here is the key idea of variation theory: Humans pay more attention to things that change than things that stay the same.
By keeping many things in the learning environment constant and varying one thing at a time, we can direct the learner's attention to the most important mathematical ideas.
great tip from Craig Barton — carry a mini whiteboard with you when you’re circulating around the room!
The number of ideas a student has to hold in their head tends to be invisible to math teachers who are experienced with that concept.
But variation theory is an especially good fit for this situation where I know a student is confused and I want to help them gain confidence and avoid overwhelming their working memory.
